find: Midway upon the journey of our life
title: Midway upon the journey of our life
note: The poem begins with a man of thirty-five lost in a wood, and the pronoun is "our".

find: All hope abandon, ye who enter in
title: The gate of Hell
note: The inscription over the gate, in Longfellow's rendering — the last line of it is the one everybody knows.

find: When that Aprilis, with his showers swoot
title: When April comes
note: Spring makes people restless, says Chaucer, and restless people go on pilgrimage. The frame for everything that follows.

find: it is much safer to be feared than loved
title: Better feared than loved
note: Machiavelli's most quoted sentence, with the qualification that is usually dropped from the quotation.

find: What do I know?
title: What do I know?
note: Montaigne's motto, struck on a medal with a pair of scales — a question, not a position.

find: because men that are free, well-born, well-bred
title: The rule of the Abbey of Thélème
note: Rabelais' imaginary abbey has one rule — Do What Thou Wilt — on the theory that well-made people need no others.

find: In a village of La Mancha
title: In a village of La Mancha
note: The first paragraph of the first modern novel, which begins by refusing to remember where it is set.

find: Now is the winter of our discontent
title: Now is the winter of our discontent
note: Richard opens the play by telling the audience exactly what he intends to do, and then does it.

find: But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks
title: The balcony scene
note: Romeo, in the dark, watching a window. Neither of them knows the other is listening.

find: The quality of mercy is not strain’d
title: The quality of mercy
note: Portia, disguised as a lawyer, argues for mercy — and then wins the case on the strictest possible reading of the law.

find: We few, we happy few, we band of brothers
title: We band of brothers
note: The English are outnumbered and ill; the king turns that into the reason to be glad they came.

find: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears
title: Friends, Romans, countrymen
note: Antony has been forbidden to blame the conspirators, and spends the speech obeying that instruction.

find: All the world’s a stage
title: The seven ages of man
note: Jaques divides a life into seven parts, and finds the last one no better than the first.

find: If music be the food of love, play on
title: If music be the food of love
note: A duke in love with being in love, which the rest of the play will not let him get away with.

find: To be, or not to be: that is the question
title: To be, or not to be
note: Not a soliloquy about revenge but about whether to go on living, spoken while he is being watched.

find: What a piece of work is a man
title: What a piece of work is a man
note: The Renaissance case for human greatness, recited by someone who has stopped believing it.

find: Put out the light, and then put out the light
title: Put out the light
note: Othello talks himself into it in the language of someone performing a duty.

find: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods
title: As flies to wanton boys
note: Gloucester, blinded, states the bleakest theology in Shakespeare.

find: Is this a dagger which I see before me
title: Is this a dagger
note: The murder has not happened yet. Macbeth is already seeing things.

find: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow
title: To-morrow, and to-morrow
note: His wife is dead and the army is at the gate; what he produces is a statement about time.

find: Our revels now are ended
title: Our revels now are ended
note: Prospero breaks off a masque to say that the world will end the same way the show did.

find: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
title: Sonnet 18
note: The argument is not that the beloved is beautiful but that the poem will outlast them both.

find: Let me not to the marriage of true minds
title: Sonnet 116
note: A definition of love written entirely as a list of what it does not do.
